The panel has three sections - Places, QGIS project and Layers. A click
on a header collapses the section, and the open sections take its place. The globe
remembers which sections are collapsed.

The section shows in one list what is on the globe now. Its check boxes
take effect at once, without the Refresh button. The rows go like this:

| Rows | What they hold |
|---|---|
| Base map | The base map - imagery or a map. A click on the row opens a menu - Esri World Imagery, OpenStreetMap, the QGIS XYZ Tiles connections and Add tile source… |
| Relief | The check box turns heights and hill shading on. A click on the name opens a menu - land heights Terrarium, Copernicus DEM 30 m, GEDTM30, ALOS AW3D30, NASADEM or USGS 3DEP 10 m, Sea and ocean depths with the depth source - the height tiles or GEBCO 2026 - and Data sources… |
| Layers that are on | Layers and the map of the catalogue, the coordinate grid, 3D buildings, contours - everything that is switched on |
| Vector base groups | Borders and names, Transport, Nature, while something in them is on |

A row takes one line. The ⋯ on the right of a row opens its menu, the
right button opens the same menu. Clearing the check box switches the
layer off, the row stays, and the same check box switches the layer on
again. The Remove from the globe item of the menu removes the row too.
The Opacity slider of the menu changes the opacity of the layer -
points, surface colouring or lines, the value is remembered. For
mineral deposits, power plants, mines, earthquakes, fires, plate
boundaries, mining areas, power lines and cables the menu also saves
what is in view to the QGIS project. The To QGIS project… item asks for a GeoPackage
file and writes the objects inside the view frame with the record
fields into it. The layer goes into the PlanetX - globe layers group at
the top of the project tree. Points keep the globe colour and size,
lines and outlines keep their style. A repeated export replaces the
earlier layer with the same name in the group. The exported layer is a
copy of a globe layer, so it does not go onto the globe by itself, in
the Layers as on the QGIS map mode too. Its check box in the QGIS project
section shows it. Colourings go to the project too.
A weather forecast field and currents go as a raster of values inside
the view frame (degrees, mm/h, m/s, for wind and currents also bands of
the eastward and northward speeds) with the globe legend. A NASA theme,
clouds and surface temperature go as a NASA GIBS image of the same date,
the temperature as two rasters - sea and land.

The Add data button at the top of the section opens the catalogue
window, see Add data catalogue. The vector base groups hold
rows. Borders and names holds Borders, Places, Water names, Rivers
and Lakes and reservoirs. Transport holds Roads, Road numbers,
Railways and Airports. Nature holds Peaks, Reserves and national
parks. Rivers and lakes are off by default.

The vector base comes from OpenFreeMap tiles. On the first opening
borders, places, terrain and stars are on. The tooltip of each row
tells how the feature is drawn and from what height it is visible.

The grid step follows the camera height, from 30° from space to
seconds near the ground. The stars stand where they stand over the
Earth at this minute and fade when the camera goes below 150 km. The
Milky Way image, about 10 MB, is downloaded when the stars are first
shown and comes from the QGIS cache afterwards. The Atmosphere row is
on by default. Without it there is no air glow at the edge of the
globe, no sky above the horizon and no haze over the distant surface,
the view background is black space.
Clouds lie as a veil over the imagery. Snow and ice get into the
clouds too, they have the same colour.

The Surface temperature map of the catalogue colours land and sea with
their own scales. The scales in degrees Celsius are in the bottom left
corner of the view. Land shows
the temperature of the surface itself by day, not of the air, over 8
days. Land may have gaps under clouds. Sea shows the water temperature
near the surface over a day.

The Sun layer lights the terrain and buildings from the side of the
sun. The night side of the Earth is dark, the air over it does not
glow. City lights shine on it - the NASA Black Marble image of 2016,
pixel about 600 m. In the twilight the lights fade together with the
night, under clouds they are weaker. The sun time is the end of the interval of the open time
slider, so the light of the hour of a placemark shows. Without the
slider the sun follows the computer clock. Without the Sun layer the
light falls from the north-west at 45°, as on a relief map. The
position of the sun is computed to about 0.01°, there are no
shadows.

Labels stay level at any turn and tilt and do not overlap. A place
behind a mountain or beyond the horizon has no label.

The Slope and Aspect layers colour the surface by the terrain heights.
Slope is the angle of the surface to the horizontal, in classes 0-2°,
2-5°, 5-10°, 10-15°, 15-25°, 25-35° and steeper than 35°, from green
to purple. Aspect is the compass direction a slope faces downhill,
each of the eight directions has its colour, ground flatter than 0.5°
is grey. The scale is in the bottom left corner of the view. The slope
is computed from the true heights, without the vertical exaggeration
of the view. The layer exists on the Earth, Mars and the Moon, other
bodies have no heights. The accuracy is limited by the height pixel.
It is about 5 m at the equator on the most detailed level on the Earth,
2.6 km on Mars, 1.3 km on the Moon.

Slope and contours are drawn no farther than three distances from the
camera to the look-at point. In a view tilted to the horizon the far
terrain stays without them. So the computation does not hold the view
on hundreds of far tiles.

The Contours layer of the Map category of the catalogue draws lines of equal height on the
surface, as on
a topographic map. The contour interval depends on the zoom. It is
1, 2, 2.5 or 5 metres times a power of ten. Close up at middle
latitudes it is 5 m, from tens of kilometres up it is 20-50 m. Every
fifth contour is thicker. Below sea level the lines are blue, these
are depth contours. Where contours merge on a steep slope, they fade.
Contours are built from the same heights as the slope and have the
same accuracy. The layer exists on the Earth, Mars and the Moon.

The interval is never finer than 5 m. The open Earth heights were
surveyed with a 20-90 m spacing, detailed tiles are their resampling.
Close up the contours are therefore built from smoothed heights with
about a 20 m spacing, resampled smoothly. The lines have no steps,
small terrain forms do not show on them. Open sea depths exist in these
data only on overview levels, so depth contours in the open sea are
built from them close up too. Own terrain from a project
raster and an own height source give contours at full detail.

Thicker contours are labelled with their height, as on a topographic
map. The number stands in a gap of the line, the top of the digits
faces uphill. There is no label at a tile edge, on a sharp bend of
the line and where the neighbouring contours are closer than the
height of the digits. A flat lake surface at a contour height does
not count as a line and is not filled.

On satellite imagery contours are yellow and depth contours light
blue, on a map they are brown and blue. Imagery means Esri World
Imagery and the imagery of other bodies. Basemaps with imagery,
satellite, aerial, ortho and similar words in the name or address
count as imagery too.

While the layer is on, its scale stands in the bottom left corner of
the view. It shows the line colour, the interval in the middle of the
view and the step of thicker contours. The cross of the scale switches
the contours off.

The To the QGIS project… link of the scale exports the contours of an
area around the view point as a GeoPackage layer. The View contours to
the QGIS project… item of the globe menu does the same. Export exists
only on the Earth.
The area is the view strip at the view point with the width and height
of the window, the interval is as on the screen. Heights are loaded for
up to 30 s. The layer goes to the PlanetX - contours group at the top
of the layer tree. The `elev` field is the height, thicker lines are
wider and labelled.

Sea and ocean depths are part of the terrain. The floor lies at its
depths, and semi-transparent water lies above it at sea level. Water
shallower than 200 m is more transparent, the floor shows near the
shore. Below sea level the status bar shows the depth under the
cursor. The depths come from the GEBCO 2026 grid with a step of about
450 m over the Terrarium tiles, coarser than level 5 - from the tiles
themselves, in the ocean these are ETOPO1 data. The menu of the Relief
row and the Data sources window choose the depth source. The depths are
not fit for navigation. Sea names stay at sea
level. The elevation profile, the ruler and the slope use the floor,
the viewshed and insolation use the water surface. A profile below
sea level shows the water and a dashed sea level line. Dry
depressions below zero, for example the Dead Sea, are not told apart
from the sea by the heights and are filled on the profile. On the
globe water lies only where the vector base map has it. The bottom of
a quarry and a dry depression below zero stay land, placemarks, paths
and labels on them stand on the relief. Until the water layer of the
base map is loaded, such a place is shown as water. The
Sea and ocean depths box in the Terrain group of the view properties
switches them off, then heights below sea level count as zero and the
sea is flat. Depths exist only on the Earth.

The Paleogeography layer shows the Earth in the past, up to 540 million
years ago, after the PALEOMAP PaleoDEM maps (Scotese and Wright, 2018).
The map of an age holds land heights and sea depths on a 0.1° grid,
about 11 km, coloured by height with hill shading. A slider in the
bottom left corner of the view sets the age in millions of years in
steps of 5 million years, the geological period is named next to it.
The ▶ button shows the ages one after another towards the present.
Today's imagery, borders, labels and relief are removed for that time,
the relief setting itself does not change. The maps lie as tiles in
the planetx-terrain repository, the first showing of an age needs the
internet. A new age appears at once in a coarse form and sharpens as
it loads. When the window opens, the row is off.

The Add data button of the Layers section opens the catalogue as a separate window over the globe. The window is not modal - the globe, the panel and the Layers list stay as they were, the catalogue can stay open. The window remembers its place and size. Sections with groups stand on the left. A click on a section shows the rows of all its groups, a click on a group shows only that group. - Base - Base maps, Local data, Map (the vector base, coordinate grid, 3D buildings, contours, cadastre), Map overlays and Encyclopedia. - Earth now - Weather, NASA themes by groups, Soils and All NASA GIBS layers. - Archive and surveys - Imagery archive (Esri Wayback, event imagery), Historical maps and Imagery at a point. - Inside the Earth - Geology (Geological map, Lithology, Earth cutaway, Paleogeography), Earthquakes and plates (Earthquakes, Historical earthquakes, Plate boundaries, Active faults, Plate motion, Volcanoes), Geophysics (Magnetic poles, Declination lines, Magnetic anomalies, Gravity anomalies, Bouguer anomalies, Geoid, Ocean floor age, Heat flow) and Commodities (Mineral deposits, Mining areas, OSM mines and quarries). - Sky - Sky and light (Stars, Atmosphere, Clouds, Sun, Satellites) and Satellites - the satellite groups. - Energy and transport - Energy (Power plants, Power lines and pipelines, Submarine cables) and Transport. - Terrain analysis - Slope, Aspect. The search field looks for a name and a description across the whole catalogue. The Windows at the look point rows are Satellite images here, Lidar point clouds here, Rumsey historical maps here and Eto Mesto old maps here. They have no check box. The Open the window button and a double click open the window of the source at the look point, as the same items of the globe menu do. The rows are split into One map on the globe and Layers - switched on together. A row has a check box, a preview, the name and the source and day of the map on a second line. The preview of a map is its tile over Eurasia on the latest ready day over the base map, forecast fields and fires show a strip of the scale colours. The check box shows a map or a layer on the globe. A click on a row shows its description under the list with the Show on the globe or Remove from the globe and To QGIS project… buttons. The globe shows one map of the catalogue, the cross on its scale in the lower left corner of the view also removes it. A satellite group card shows or removes the group. The first group switches the Satellites layer on, the last removed one switches it off. NASA themes are rasters by days, months or years from the NASA GIBS service. A day of a series counts as ready a day later, before that its image is empty. The NASA theme groups of the catalogue hold: - Planet of Fire - fire spots, smoke, aerosol optical depth, carbon monoxide and its emission. - Planet of Water - precipitation, soil moisture, daily snow, snow over 8 days, snow mass, sea ice, water vapour, chlorophyll, sea salinity and floods. - Planet of Air - nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, methane, carbon dioxide and ozone. - Land and Life - vegetation, dust and night lights. The theme lies as semi-transparent colouring over the imagery, where there is no data the imagery shows. A legend with the name, units and date stands in the bottom left corner of the view. The day of the theme is set by the right handle of the time slider, see Placemark time and the time slider. A chosen theme opens the slider on the last day of its series. The handle gives the nearest day of the series that is not later, missing days of the series are skipped. A new theme takes the same moment while the slider is open. Some series lag behind today by months, the tooltip of the theme says so. Themes exist only on the Earth. Daily snow from MODIS imagery shows only where the day had no clouds and was light. On 15 January 2026 over West Siberia clouds and the polar night hid snow on 78 % of the area. The 8-day summary is hidden on 40 %. Snow mass is a SMAP model calculation from satellite data, it has no gaps under clouds. The snow themes show land only. Lake ice is in the 8-day summary, sea ice is the Sea ice theme. The All NASA GIBS layers category shows the whole catalogue of the service - more than a thousand raster imagery and map layers. The list comes from the GIBS catalogue on the first showing of the category or on a search of three characters or more, the first time in about 10 seconds. The Find field finds a layer by all words of the query, for example "snow cover daily terra", the layer titles are in English. These rows are not shown in All. A catalogue layer behaves as a theme - one map on the globe, a date series and the timeline, a colour scale, the day swipe. JPEG imagery, for example "Corrected Reflectance (True Color, MODIS, Terra)", lies without transparency. Layers without a date series show one picture. The globe remembers the chosen layer after a restart too. Layers with a step shorter than a day and GIBS vector layers are not in the list.

The ⇆ button of the time slider splits the view with a swipe. Right
of the swipe the theme is shown for the day of the slider, left of it
for a day of its own. By default this is the same day a year ago, for
a series shorter than a year its first day. Tags with the days of both
sides stand above the swipe. The ‹ and › buttons of the left tag move
its day along the theme series, the cross removes the swipe. The swipe
is dragged with the mouse by the strip with a circle.

The white line along the border is also on a view snapshot and in
a tour recording. The swipe works with NASA themes. GFS forecast
fields, fires and surface temperature have no swipe. A change of
theme keeps the swipe, its day is looked up in the series of the new
theme. Switching the theme off removes the swipe.

The Esri Wayback map of the Imagery archive category in the catalog
shows past releases of the Esri World Imagery basemap. The releases
start on 20 February 2014, in October 2026 there are 197 of them. The
map opens the time slider at the latest release. The right handle
selects the release not later than its day.

The ‹ and › steps of the slider go only through the releases in which
the image at the centre of the view changed. When the view has stood
still for 0.7 s, the plugin asks the Esri service which release the
tile at the centre of the view actually comes from. The closer the
view, the smaller this tile. At the centre of Perm from 3 km there are
12 such releases out of 197. Until the service answers, the steps go
through all releases.

The ⇆ swipe compares two releases in the same way as two days of a
NASA theme. By default the left part shows the release a year earlier.

The release date is not the capture date. What's here? and the
Identify features mode give the Esri Wayback imagery archive group -
the capture date, the provider, the imaging system, the resolution and
the accuracy of the release image at the clicked point. Add to QGIS
project… of the On the globe row adds the release as an XYZ tile
layer, no file is written.

The terms are the same as for Esri World Imagery, see Data sources.

The Disaster imagery map of the Imagery archive category shows imagery
of earthquakes, floods, wildfires and hurricanes from two open
catalogs. Vantor (formerly Maxar) provides WorldView strips, Planet
provides PlanetScope, SkySat and Pelican scenes and the quarterly
Planet basemap before the event. On 25 October 2026 the catalogs hold
18 events - 11 from Vantor and 7 from Planet. No key is needed.

The map opens the Disaster imagery window with a list of events. A row
shows the event, the date and the source, below the list is the
catalog description. The Search bar
also opens the window by the words disaster imagery, earthquake, flood
and the like. Show on the globe loads the list of the event images,
flies to the event and opens the time slider at the last imagery day.
The earthquake in Colombia on 10 August 2026 has 164 images over
5 days.

The right handle of the slider selects the day. The globe shows all
images not later than that day, newer ones over older ones. The ‹
and › steps go through the imagery days. If the event has images from
before it, the ⇆ swipe turns on at once. The left part shows the last
day before the event, the right part the slider day. The images come
from cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs in parts, only what is in view. The
first display of a large event takes several minutes.

Add to QGIS project… of the On the globe row adds the images of the
day within the view as network rasters to the PlanetX - disaster
imagery group, at most 12 images, no files are written. Remove from
the globe in the window takes the imagery away.

The imagery licence is CC BY-NC 4.0. It allows only non-commercial
use and requires the Vantor or Planet Labs PBC credit. It is
shown in the corner of the view.

The Weather category stands in the catalogue before the NASA themes. Its first map is Surface temperature of land and sea from NASA. The others are Air temperature at 2 m, Precipitation, GFS forecast in mm/h, Wind at 10 m in m/s and Cloud cover, GFS forecast in percent. Precipitation from satellite imagery is the Precipitation, IMERG satellites row of Planet of Water. The fields come from the NOAA GFS forecast model with a 0.25° grid, about 28 km. A field is chosen in the catalogue, as a NASA theme. The Aurora map shows the probability of a visible aurora in percent by the OVATION forecast of the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center for the next 30-90 minutes, 1° grid. Below 3 % the field is transparent, a weak aurora is green, a strong one yellow and red. There is one forecast, for now, the time slider does not change it. The map asks for a new forecast at most once in 10 minutes. City lights on the night side come with the Sun layer, they can be on together with the aurora. White streaks run over the Wind colouring - particles that float with the wind and drag a trail. A streak of a weak wind is paler. The streaks are sped up - in a second a wind of typical strength passes about an eighth of the view width, so they are visible both from afar and close up. They are born within the view and follow it. The Currents layer of the Planet of water group of the catalogue shows ocean surface currents with the same white streaks over a speed colouring from dark blue for slow ones to red for 2.5 m/s. Slow water is almost not coloured, the streak of a slow current is paler. From afar the particles are born within the visible circle of the Earth and pass no more than a third of a grid cell per frame, so the trail does not loop through the eddies. The currents are geostrophic, NOAA CoastWatch calculates them from satellite altimetry for a day, the data lag two to three weeks. The series starts on 13 February 2017, the day of the currents is set by the right handle of the time slider, without the slider it is the latest ready day. The 0.25° grid is taken at every other node, 0.5°. The first switch-on in a QGIS session downloads about 4 MB. The Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, the current around Antarctica and eddies tens of kilometres across are visible. Near the coasts and under ice there is no data. The time slider sets the moment of the field. A chosen field opens the slider at the present moment. The slider spans 10 days before the latest model run and 16 days of forecast after it. The future is the forecast of the latest run, hourly for the first 5 days, then every 3 hours. The past is the model analysis for the nearest hour. The ‹ and › buttons of the slider move the moment by an hour, ▶ shows the hours one after another and waits for each to load. The model runs 4 times a day, a new run is published 4-5 hours later. A field for the whole world weighs 0.5-0.8 MB and arrives in a few seconds. The legend in the bottom left corner shows the units and the valid time of the field in UTC. It is a model calculation. Model clouds are not a cloud image, the Clouds layer gives the image. The values of the field stand over its colours. Temperature is in degrees, precipitation in mm/h, wind in m/s, clouds in percent. The values stand at the nodes of a latitude and longitude grid, about six across the view. The node step changes with the eye height, from 30° from space to 0.25° close up. The values come from the same field, there are no new network requests. Where precipitation is below 0.1 mm/h, there are no precipitation values. The first map of the Planet of Fire is Fires. It shows fire spots over the last 24 hours from VIIRS images of the NOAA-20 satellite from the NASA FIRMS feed, about 78 thousand spots. A dot stands at the fire, its colour and size show the radiative power from 1 to 1000 MW, the legend stands in the bottom left corner of the view. The feed, about 6 MB, is loaded each time the row is switched on. The spots stand on the time slider by the image time. A click on a spot in the Identify mode shows its power, image time and confidence. The Plate boundaries layer shows the lithospheric plate boundaries after the PB2002 model (Bird, 2003). Red lines are plates moving apart at oceanic ridges and continental rifts, green - plates sliding along transform faults, blue - plates converging in subduction and collision zones. Plate names show as labels. A click near a boundary in the Identify mode shows the boundary type, the plate pair and the speed of their relative motion in mm/yr. In the plate pair a slash in Bird's notation shows which plate goes under which. "PA\OK" is the Pacific plate under the Okhotsk plate. The Active faults layer shows about 13.7 thousand faults of the world from the GEM Global Active Faults database (Styron and Pagani, 2020) compiled from regional catalogues. The line colour shows the kind of slip. Blue lines are normal faults, red ones reverse faults, thrusts and subduction zones, green ones strike-slip faults, orange ones spreading ridges, purple ones folds, grey ones have no kind given. The legend stands in the lower left corner of the view. A click on a line shows the name, the kind of slip, the database entry, the slip rate in mm/yr, the dip and the source catalogue. The database file, about 11 MB, is downloaded on the first switch-on and kept in the QGIS profile. The database licence is CC BY-SA 4.0. The Magnetic poles layer shows the north and south magnetic poles - the points where a compass needle stands vertical. The red point is the north pole, the blue one is the south pole, each trails its path since 1590. The time slider opens by itself. The right handle moves the poles over the years, the left one cuts the start of the path - the path starts at the year of the left handle. The positions of 1590-2025 come from the NOAA NCEI tables (the gufm1 and IGRF models), after 2025 the pole is computed with the IGRF-14 model up to 2030. A click on the globe in the Identify mode shows in the Magnetic field group the declination - the angle between compass north and geographic north, the inclination and the field intensity at the point for the slider year. The field is computed with the IGRF-14 model for 1900-2030 and with the gufm1 model (Jackson et al., 2000) for 1590-1899. The gufm1 file, about 1 MB, is downloaded from the authors' site on the first request for a year before 1900, until it arrives the window shows only the year. From 1900 to 2025 the north pole shifted 2475 km in a straight line, from the Canadian Arctic towards Siberia. The Declination lines layer shows lines of equal magnetic declination every 10° for the year of the right handle of the time slider. The slider opens by itself, as for the poles. Red lines mean east declination, blue lines west declination, the green line zero declination, where the compass points to geographic north. Labels on the lines give the declination in degrees. The lines converge at the magnetic poles. They are computed with the same gufm1 and IGRF-14 models on a 2° grid, from 1590 to 2030. In 1800 the declination near London was about 24° west, by 2020 it came close to zero. The Plate motion layer shows arrows of the motion of lithospheric plates after the NNR-MORVEL56 model (Argus, Gordon and DeMets, 2011) - the velocity relative to the mean motion of all plates. The arrows stand at grid nodes, about seven across the view, the grid step changes with the eye height. The arrow length grows with the speed, the number at the arrow start is the speed in mm/yr. The plate at a point is found from the PB2002 outlines. The Pacific plate near Hawaii moves northwest at about 70 mm/yr, the Eurasian plate at about 25 mm/yr. A click in the Identify mode shows the plate, speed and direction of motion in the Place group. The Volcanoes layer shows about 1200 volcanoes that erupted during the last 12 thousand years, after the list of the Global Volcanism Program of the Smithsonian Institution. The point colour shows the time of the last eruption. A red point means an eruption after 1900, orange - from 1500 to 1899, yellow - earlier, grey - the time is unknown. The point size grows with the volcano height. The legend stands in the lower left corner of the view. A click on a point shows the name, volcano type, height, year of the last eruption, tectonic setting and a link to the volcano page on the GVP site. The list is downloaded on the first switch-on, about 2 MB, and kept as a file in the QGIS profile. The Magnetic anomalies layer shows the departure of the Earth magnetic field from the normal one after the NOAA NCEI EMAG2v3 grid at 4 km above the ellipsoid, a grid step of about 4 km. Red places mean a stronger field than normal, blue a weaker one, the legend in the corner of the view runs from -250 to +250 nT. The anomalies reveal the crust, for example the Kursk magnetic anomaly, the stripes of the ocean floor on both sides of the mid-ocean ridges, ancient shields. Where there is no survey the layer is empty. A click in the Identify mode shows the value at the point, near Kursk about +270 nT. The tiles lie in the planetx-terrain repository, about 50 MB for the whole world, and load as they are shown. The Gravity anomalies, Bouguer anomalies, Ocean floor age and Heat flow layers are value maps, like the magnetic anomalies. The globe shows one value map at a time, switching on another one removes the previous one. Each has its own legend in the corner of the view, a click in the Identify mode shows the value at the point. The tiles lie in the planetx-terrain repository and load as they are shown. The Geological map layer shows the Macrostrat geological map of the world (University of Wisconsin-Madison) compiled from maps of different scales. The colour shows the age of the rocks on the stratigraphic scale. From afar the overview map of the world is visible, closer up - detailed maps where they exist. In Russia and Europe the most detailed map is the International Geological Map of Europe 1:5 000 000, in the USA the maps are much more detailed. Deeper than the most detailed map of a place the tiles are empty, and the enlarged coarser map stays on the screen. A click in the Identify mode shows in the Geology group the unit, the lithology, the age on the scale and in Ma, the source map and a link to the Macrostrat page at the point. Near Perm these are Permian clays, 274-252 Ma, after the map of Europe. The geological map shares its place with the geophysical value maps, the globe shows one of them. Add to QGIS project… of the On the globe row adds the map as an XYZ tile layer. The Macrostrat data are CC BY 4.0. The Lithology layer shows the GLiM lithological map of the world (Hartmann and Moosdorf, 2012) - surface rocks in 16 classes. These are unconsolidated sediments, siliciclastic, mixed and carbonate sedimentary rocks, evaporites, pyroclastics, acid, intermediate and basic volcanic and plutonic rocks, metamorphic rocks, ice and glaciers. The map is compiled from 92 regional maps at a scale of about 1:3 750 000. The class legend sits in the lower left corner of the view. A click in the Identify mode shows the rock class at the point in the Lithology group. The tiles are kept in the planetx-terrain repository. Like the geological map, the lithology shares its place with the geophysical value maps. The Historical earthquakes layer shows the ISC-GEM catalogue - about 74 thousand strong earthquakes of the world from 1904 to 2024 of magnitude 5 and above, with locations, depths and moment magnitudes recomputed in one way. The circles stand as in the Earthquakes layer, the colour shows the depth and the size the magnitude. The catalogue enters the time slider range, and its handles select the events by year. A click on a circle shows the place, date, magnitude, depth and a link to the USGS event page. The first use downloads the catalogue in parts, about 13 MB, and keeps it as a file in the QGIS profile. The catalogue licence is CC BY-SA 3.0. The Land cover layer of the Earth and life group shows the ESA WorldCover map for 2021 from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 images with a 10 m pixel. There are 11 classes - forest, shrubland, grassland, cropland, built-up, bare and sparse vegetation, snow and ice, permanent water bodies, herbaceous wetland, mangroves, moss and lichen. The class legend sits in the lower left corner of the view. From afar the map comes from the planetx-terrain repository, close up from the Microsoft Planetary Computer service. A click in the Identify mode shows the class at the point. The map licence is CC BY 4.0. The Water occurrence and Water transitions layers of the Planet of water group show the JRC Global Surface Water dataset (Pekel et al., 2016) from Landsat images of 1984-2021 with a 30 m pixel. Occurrence is the share of observations when the place was under water, from red (rarely) to blue (always). Transitions divide water into classes - permanent and seasonal water, new and lost, seasonal to permanent and back, and ephemeral water. They show new reservoirs, shrunken lakes such as the Aral Sea, and migrating channels. A click in the Identify mode shows the occurrence in percent or the class. The layers of the Soils group - Clay in soil, Sand in soil, Soil organic carbon and Soil pH - show properties of the soil layer 0-5 cm from ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0, a model built on soil profiles of the world with a 250 m grid. Clay and sand are in percent, organic carbon in g/kg, pH is measured in water. The pictures come from the SoilGrids WMS service, and a click in the Identify mode asks it for the value at the point. Water and places without data are transparent. The SoilGrids licence is CC BY 4.0. The globe shows one map out of the lithological, geological, water, soil and geophysical value maps, turning on another one removes the previous one. Add to QGIS project… of the On the globe row adds such a map to the project as an XYZ tile layer or a WMS layer of the service. The Gravity anomalies layer shows the free-air gravity anomaly - the departure of gravity from the normal one after the XGM2019e model (Zingerle et al., 2020), computed to degree 719, a step of about 28 km. Red places mean gravity above normal, blue below normal, the legend runs from -200 to +200 mGal. Over deep-sea trenches the anomaly drops to -300 mGal, near the Mariana Trench to about -305 mGal, over Hawaii it rises to +370 mGal. Seamounts show as red spots. The Bouguer anomalies layer shows the same anomaly minus the attraction of the relief - the simple Bouguer correction 2πGρh after the NOAA ETOPO 2022 relief. Rock above sea level is removed with a density of 2670 kg/m³, ice with 917 kg/m³, water and ice below sea level are replaced by rock. The correction is computed on 1' cells and averaged to 0.25° cells. The terrain correction for the surrounding relief within 167 km is added to it - mountains and valleys near the point, 10 to 25 mGal per cell in mountains and almost 0 on plains. Under mountains the anomaly is negative, about -510 mGal at Tibet and about -155 mGal at the Alps - this is the thick light crust beneath them. Over the ocean it is positive, about +330 mGal in the middle of the Pacific. The legend runs from -400 to +400 mGal. The Ocean floor age layer shows the age of the oceanic crust after the grid of Seton et al. 2020, a 0.1° step. Young floor at mid-ocean ridges is red, old floor at ocean margins is blue and purple, the oldest floor, about 180 Ma, lies in the western Pacific. Land and continental crust are not coloured. The Heat flow layer shows the heat flow from the interior through the Earth's surface in mW/m² on a 0.5° grid built by kriging from 91 thousand measurements of the IHFC 2024 database. Blue places are cold old shields, red ones are rifts, mid-ocean ridges and volcanic areas, near Yellowstone about 180 mW/m². Far from measurements the grid is smoothed. The Geoid layer shows the shape of the geoid - the Earth level surface from which heights above sea level are counted - after the NGA EGM2008 model. While the row is on, the globe heights are the geoid heights above the ellipsoid, from -107 to +86 m, stretched 10 000 times, and the Earth looks crumpled. Bulges stand where gravity is stronger, for example near New Guinea and in the North Atlantic, hollows where it is weaker, the deepest one south of India. Terrain, water and the haze over the surface are removed for this time, the atmosphere glow at the edge of the globe stays. The Scale slider in the ⋯ menu of the Geoid row stretches the heights from 1000 to 20 000 times. The Earth cutaway in this mode reaches the crumpled surface, all shells are stretched in the same proportion. Switching the row off brings back terrain, scale and sea depths. A click in the Identify mode shows the geoid height above the ellipsoid at the point in the Geoid group. The Mineral deposits layer shows mineral deposits, mines and occurrences of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) from three datasets. The MRDS database is about 300 thousand points, about 267 thousand of them in the USA and about 1400 in Russia, USGS has not updated it since 2011. Major mineral deposits of the world (USGS OFR 2005-1294) is 3161 deposits, 300 of them in Russia, they show as large points. World mines and plants (USGS Mineral operations outside the United States) is 6478 mines, processing and metallurgical plants outside the USA for 2006-2010 with the operator and capacity, among them the Verkhnekamsk deposit, the North Urals bauxite and the Saranovsky chromite complex. For some records the place is given by district, the information window then says approximate, by district. The point colour is the group of the first commodity, the group scale is in the lower left corner of the view. The size of an MRDS point is the development status, a producing mine is larger than an occurrence. A click on a point shows the name, commodities, type, status, operator, capacity, country and a link to the USGS record, the Identify mode is not needed for it. Earthquake foci, fires and satellites open the same way. The first switch-on downloads the USGS archives, about 25 MB, and parses them in a background thread, which takes 15-20 s. The result is kept as a file in the QGIS profile, later switch-ons read it in 1-2 s. Over a large area, for example the whole USA, no more than 80 thousand points show. The major deposits, world mines and plants come first, then the rest. Large points are drawn over small ones. The Mining areas layer shows outlines of open pits, waste dumps, tailings and industrial sites of the world - about 45 thousand areas outlined on Sentinel-2 images of 2019 (Maus et al., 2022, CC BY-SA 4.0). The outlines lie as an orange fill in the tile image. A click on an outline shows the country and area. The first switch-on downloads a file of about 25 MB into the QGIS profile. The OSM mines and quarries layer shows mines, shafts and quarries from OpenStreetMap with their names. They load for the place of the view when the camera is below 150 km - an area of about 100 km around the look point in one request to an Overpass server. The point colour is the commodity group from the resource tag, without it the point is white, Other. A click on a point shows the name, kind, operator and a link to the OpenStreetMap object. In busy hours the Overpass server answers with a delay or a refusal. The request then repeats by itself on another Overpass server or on the same one after a pause. The Energy category of the catalogue holds the Power plants, OSM power lines, cables and pipelines and Submarine cables layers. The Submarine cables layer shows submarine communication lines in turquoise and submarine power cables in purple from any altitude. The data is OpenStreetMap, extracted on 11 October 2026 - 909 communication lines and 1040 power cables longer than 5 km. OSM holds part of the world's cables, most of them in the Atlantic and near Europe. A click on a line shows the name, kind, owner and a link to the OpenStreetMap object. The Power plants layer shows about 35 thousand power plants of the world from the WRI Global Power Plant Database, data as of 2021 (CC BY 4.0). The point colour is the fuel, the size is the capacity. The points are visible from any altitude, a click on a point shows the name, capacity, commissioning year, owner and a link to the source of the record. Some plants are placed wrongly in the database. The first switch-on downloads an archive of about 4 MB, the result is kept as a file in the QGIS profile. The OSM power lines, cables and pipelines layer shows power lines, substations, cables and pipelines from OpenStreetMap. A power cable, underground or under water, is a purple dashed line, a communication line is turquoise. The line colour and width show the voltage class - 500 kV and above, 220-330 kV, 110-150 kV or below. A pipeline is dashed, its colour shows the substance - gas, oil and products, water and heat. A substation is a square in the colour of its voltage. The objects load for the place of the view when the camera is below 150 km, the same way as the OSM mines. A click on a line or substation shows the kind, voltage, substance, owner and a link to the OpenStreetMap object. The Earthquakes layer shows earthquakes of magnitude 4.5 and above over the last 30 days from the feed of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). The feed is loaded each time the row is switched on. A circle marks the epicentre on the surface. The colour of the circle shows the focus depth, from red near the surface to purple at 700 km, the scale is in the bottom left corner of the view. The circle grows with the magnitude. Foci on the far side of the Earth are hidden. A focus is seen at its depth in the removed sector of the Earth cutaway row - there the circle sits at the focus. The depth is stretched by the vertical exaggeration of the terrain, like the heights. Each event has a time. With the row on, the time slider becomes available, and it shows the events of the chosen interval. The row exists only on the Earth. The Earth cutaway layer removes a sector of the Earth under the look-at point. The sector is a quarter of a hemisphere 90° wide in longitude, from the equator to the pole of the hemisphere of the look-at point. Its three faces are coloured by shells after the radii of the PREM model. These are the crust to 24.4 km, the upper mantle to 400 km, the transition zone to 670 km, the lower mantle to 2891 km, the outer core to 5149.5 km and the inner core. The shell scale is in the bottom left corner of the view. The edge of the faces lies on the ellipsoid, the depths are not stretched by the vertical exaggeration. The crust on the faces comes from the CRUST1.0 model in 1° cells. These are water, ice, upper, middle and lower sediments, upper, middle and lower crust, below the Moho the mantle begins. The crust is 6-7 km thick under the ocean and about 70 km under Tibet. Continental and oceanic crust have different colours, the oceanic crust is grey-green. The crust type comes from the P-wave speed in the upper crust of the same model. In the oceanic crust it is below 5.5 km/s, these are basalts. Where a face crosses a subduction zone, the subducting slab from the Slab2 model of the U.S. Geological Survey shows on it as a band from the upper surface of the slab down by its thickness. Slabs exist in 27 zones. The file of a zone is requested when a face touches it, the loading icon shows this. The model is downloaded from the site of its authors when the row is first switched on, until then the crust is the 24.4 km PREM layer. If the model has not arrived, the first row of the scale names the reason, and the crust stays a layer of constant thickness. The next time the row is switched on, the model is requested again. The received archive is saved to the PlanetX folder of the QGIS profile, later sessions take it from there without the network. If the authors' site does not answer, the archive crust1.0.tar.gz can be downloaded with a browser from https://igppweb.ucsd.edu/~gabi/crust1/crust1.0.tar.gz and put into this folder under the same name, then the Earth cutaway row is switched off and on. QGIS opens the profile folder with the menu item Settings - User Profiles - Open Active Profile Folder, the PlanetX folder lies in it. The crust layers can be told apart up close, where the depths on the faces are true. As the camera moves away, depths to 400 km are stretched so that the crust stays visible. At the surface the stretch reaches 8 times, towards 400 km it fades out, below the scale is true. The shell scale shows the factor, earthquake foci are stretched the same way. The Stretch the crust item of the «⋯» menu of the Earth cutaway row in the Layers section turns the stretch off, then all depths are true at any distance. The Mantle tomography item of the same menu colours the mantle on the faces after seismic tomography - the deviation of the shear wave speed from the PREM model after the SEISGLOB2 model (Durand et al., 2017). Red mantle is slower and usually hotter, blue mantle is faster and colder, the legend runs from -2 to +2 %. Slow columns show under Iceland and Hawaii, a fast sinking slab under Japan, and two large slow regions at the core boundary under Africa and the Pacific. The model is downloaded from the EarthScope site on the first switch-on, about 28 MB, and kept as a file in the QGIS profile. The crust and the core on the faces keep their colours. The CRUST1.0 crust to the QGIS project item of the same menu writes the crust surfaces within the view frame into a chosen folder - GeoTIFF rasters of elevations in metres above sea level with a 1° step. There are seven surfaces - the tops of the upper, middle and lower sediments, the tops of the upper, middle and lower crust and the Moho. The rasters go into the project as the PlanetX - CRUST1.0 crust group. The sediment and crust layers of CRUST1.0 are set apart by seismic wave speed, they are not stratigraphy. Where a layer is absent, its top matches the top of the next one. Near Perm, for example, the top of the upper crust lies at -3850 m and the Moho at -40 870 m. The rasters can be shown on the globe with the Surface by elevations item of the raster menu. Labels of places in the removed sector are not shown. The sector is placed anew each time the row is switched on. The corners of the sector are marked with points showing their latitude and longitude, and they can be dragged with the mouse. A corner changes its own longitude and its own latitude. If the latitude is neither 0° nor a pole, the lower or upper face becomes a cone towards the centre of the Earth. The row exists only on the Earth. The Section down… item in the menu of a path in My Places opens the Section window. It shows a section of the Earth down along the path. The distance from the start of the path runs across, the depth runs down. The section shows the CRUST1.0 crust layers, the PREM shells, the Slab2 slabs and earthquake foci from a band along the path. The colours are those of the Earth cutaway faces, the layer scale is to the right of the chart. The Depth list sets the depth of the section, from 100 km to the centre of the Earth. The Foci band field sets the width of the band. A focus is moved onto the section at the nearest point of the path. While the Historical earthquakes row is on, the foci of the ISC-GEM catalogue since 1904 are put onto the section too. They have a light outline and lie under the foci of the 30-day feed, the line under the chart counts them separately. With the time slider open, the section shows only the foci of its interval, as on the globe. The section is rebuilt when the handles stop. The cursor over the chart marks the point on the globe and shows the Moho and slab depths there. The crust, the slabs and the earthquake feed are loaded when the window opens, if they are not there yet, the line under the chart tells what is still loading. While the window is open, a wall of the same section hangs along the path on the globe. It shows through the surface, its depths are true. When the window closes, the wall disappears.
Base map and a tile source of your own

The menu of the Base map row lists Esri World Imagery, OpenStreetMap,
the added ready sources and the XYZ Tiles connections of the QGIS
browser, the chosen base map is checked. A choice changes the base map
on the globe at once. On other bodies the row shows the imagery of the
body, there is no choice.

All base maps with previews are gathered in the Base maps category of
the Add data catalog, a click on a row sets the base map of the globe.
The More base maps… item of the Base map menu opens the catalog on
this category. The Local data category of the same catalog holds
detailed imagery of separate areas from the services of their owners.
The first row is the spring 2020 orthophoto of nine counties around
Philadelphia (PASDA DVRPC 2020). The row sets the base map, outside
the area the globe shows Esri imagery.

The ready sources of the Base maps category are set with one click:

| Source | What it shows | Warning |
|---|---|---|
| Google Satellite, Hybrid, Map, Terrain | imagery, imagery with labels, map, map with hill shading | yes |
| Bing Aerial, Map | Microsoft imagery and map | yes |
| Yandex Satellite, Map | Yandex imagery and map | yes |
| 2GIS Map | city map | yes |
| OpenTopoMap | topographic map from OpenStreetMap and SRTM, up to level 17 | no |
| Esri World Topo Map | Esri topographic map | no |
| Esri World Street Map, Light Gray Canvas, Dark Gray Canvas, National Geographic, Ocean, World Terrain, Shaded Relief, Physical, World Hillshade | Esri maps, the ocean, terrain and shaded relief maps up to level 13, the physical map up to 8 | no |
| OSM Humanitarian, OSM France, CyclOSM | maps from OpenStreetMap - humanitarian, French and cycling | no |
| NASA Blue Marble | cloud-free image of the Earth with shaded relief and depths, up to level 8 | no |
| USGS Imagery, Imagery Topo, Topo, Shaded Relief | maps of the US National Map, the USA only, up to level 16 | no |

The terms of Google, Bing, Yandex and 2GIS do not allow taking their
tiles into third-party programs by the direct address. Before the first
addition of such a source the window says so and gives a link to the
service terms. The source is added only by the Add button, the decision
and the responsibility for its use stay with the user. The window keeps
the answer and does not ask a second time. Yandex imagery is made in
another projection, the elliptical Mercator. The plugin builds a globe
tile from two Yandex tiles and recomputes it by latitude, otherwise near
Perm the imagery would lie 36 km south of its place. An added ready
source stands in the base map list and in the Data sources window, where
the Remove button takes it out of the list. The Search line finds ready
sources too - by name, for example yandex or bing.

The assistant sets a base map as well - a ready source or a template
address of your own, if asked, for example, "set Bing imagery". A ready
source goes through the same warning, an address of your own is first
shown to the user and added only after the Yes answer.

The Map overlays category of the Add data catalog lays transparent
maps over the base map - OpenSeaMap sea marks, Waymarked Trails hiking
and cycling routes. Several can be on at once, the opacity is in the ⋯
menu of the row, To QGIS project… adds an XYZ tile layer. Sea marks are
seen close up, from the scale of about 1:500 000.

The Add tile source… item of the menu opens the new source window. The Address
field takes an address in any of these forms:

- a template with `{z}`, `{x}`, `{y}`, for example
  `https://{s}.tile.opentopomap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png`
- the address of one tile copied from a browser, for example
  `https://server.arcgisonline.com/ArcGIS/rest/services/World_Topo_Map/MapServer/tile/5/10/17`
- an address with the level, column and row in the query
- the address of a WMS service, for example
  `https://imagery.pasda.psu.edu/arcgis/services/pasda/DVRPC2020/MapServer/WMSServer`

The window turns the address into a template and suggests a name from
the server name. Below it builds a mosaic of the whole world from four
level 1 tiles. If north is at the bottom of the mosaic, the server
rows go from the bottom up, the box Rows from the bottom up (TMS)
fixes this. The window finds the most detailed level itself by asking
for tiles at the look point of the globe. No-data placeholders do not
count. The source credit is in the corner of the view and on
snapshots, for known servers it is filled in by itself.

The source is saved as a QGIS XYZ Tiles connection and becomes the
base map at once. It is also visible in the QGIS browser, where it can
be edited or removed. The owner of the tiles sets their terms of use.

The window recognises a WMS service address by the words `WMSServer`,
`/wms` or `service=WMS` and reads the layer list of the service
(GetCapabilities). The layer is chosen in the Layer list. The All
layers row shows all layers of the group together. Instead of the
mosaic the window shows one picture of the layer extent. The globe asks
the service for a picture of every tile in the Web Mercator projection
(EPSG:3857). Many services cover only their own area. Outside the layer
extent and at small scales the globe shows Esri World Imagery, at the
edge of the area the service picture lies over it. Such a source is
kept in the PlanetX settings, not as a QGIS connection. It can be
edited or removed in the Data sources window. A WMS service draws every
picture anew, so a base map from it loads slower than tiles.

The Rosreestr cadastre row of the Map category of the Add data catalogue
puts over the imagery the land parcels from the National spatial data
system of Rosreestr (NSPD, nspd.gov.ru) - borders in red, parcels with a
pale fill. Data exist only for Russia. Parcels are seen up close, from
about 10 km and lower. Coarser tiles are not requested, they hold
thousands of parcels. The service refuses frequent requests in a row, so
the plugin asks for tiles one at a time with a 0.5 s pause, the view
fills with parcels in 30-60 s. The NSPD server certificate is issued by
the certification centre of the Russian Ministry of Digital Development,
which Windows does not trust by default. The Ministry root certificate
lies in the plugin and acts only on the plugin requests to nspd.gov.ru,
it is not installed into the system or the rest of QGIS. The layer
opacity is set by the slider of its row in the Layers list. The credit
Rosreestr NSPD is in the corner of the view.

With the cadastre on, a click in the Identify features mode or the What's
here? item of the globe menu asks NSPD about the parcel under the
point. The Features window shows the Rosreestr cadastre group. It holds
the cadastral number, the address, the area, the land category and the
permitted use. It also holds the form of ownership, the type of right,
the cadastral value with its dates, the status and the cadastral block.
The parcel outline is highlighted on the globe. The NSPD map row leads
to this parcel on the Rosreestr map. A double click on a row of the
Features window copies the value, for example the cadastral number, to
the clipboard and opens a link in the browser. One request goes per
click, the information arrives in 1-3 s.

The 3D buildings row of the Layers section puts OpenStreetMap buildings on the globe as blocks. Outlines and heights come from the same OpenFreeMap vector tiles as the vector base. The row is off by default. Buildings show when the camera is closer than 6 km to the ground. The globe keeps up to 32 building tiles around the camera, the nearest first. Tiles behind the camera are not loaded. The height of a building is its height in OpenStreetMap, otherwise the number of floors times 3.66 m. A building without either gets a height of 5 m. In the centre of Perm two thirds of the buildings have a height of their own, in the centre of Moscow almost all. In the outskirts many houses have the same height. The colour of a building comes from OpenStreetMap, otherwise the building is light grey. Roofs are flat. The bottom of a building stands at the lowest point of the terrain under its outline. A view snapshot waits until all buildings of the frame are loaded. A scene remembers whether buildings are on. The 3D buildings list in the Own vector base group of the Data sources window switches the source of buildings to Overture Maps. These are OpenStreetMap buildings together with the open sets of Microsoft, Google Open Buildings and Esri in one PMTiles archive. Where OpenStreetMap is incomplete, there are more buildings. Over Lagos the same 22 tiles hold 158 thousand Overture buildings, the base has about 45 thousand in half of these tiles. The height of an Overture building is its height field, otherwise the number of floors times 3.66 m. The globe takes the latest Overture release from its catalogue. The Overture credit stands in the corner of the view while its buildings are on the globe.

The View properties icon on the icon bar opens the View properties window. The window does not block work with the globe. | Group | Field | What it sets | |---|---|---| | Base map | List | Source of imagery or map | | Terrain | Vertical exaggeration | Height multiplier from 0.5 to 10 | | Terrain | Sea and ocean depths | The floor at its depths with water above it, on by default | | Labels | Language | Language of labels and search | | QGIS map | Synchronization | Direction of the link with the map | | QGIS map | Layers as on the QGIS map | The globe shows the layers switched on in the QGIS legend | | QGIS map | New layers straight to the globe | A new project layer is checked on the globe at once | | Update | Update automatically | The globe refreshes after every change without the Refresh button, on by default | | Coordinates | Format | Decimal degrees, degrees-minutes-seconds, UTM or MGRS in the status line and the Features window. North of 84° and south of 80° UTM and MGRS are replaced with decimal degrees | | Look | Look | Dark (the default) - dark plates on the view and dark module windows. Light - grey plates with dark icons and light windows. As in QGIS - dark plates, module windows in the QGIS look. The look changes at once | | Inside the Earth | Subsurface mode… | Opens the Subsurface mode window, see [Subsurface mode](#subsurface-mode) | The default base map is Esri World Imagery, listed as an example. Esri sets its terms of use. OpenStreetMap comes next, then the XYZ Tiles connections from the QGIS browser. Terrain connections are not listed. A new connection appears in the list the next time the window opens. The Data sources… button next to the base map list opens a window with all globe sources. Its table lists by groups the base maps, terrain, vector base, NASA data and Earth science data. Each source shows what it gives and an open link to its terms of use. The Check button requests one tile or file from each source bypassing the cache and writes the answer time and size or an error. Large files, the star sky image, are not requested. The same window sets own terrain - a height tile template with {z}, {x}, {y} in Terrarium or Mapbox Terrain-RGB encoding - and an own vector base - a TileJSON address in the OpenMapTiles schema. Each has a credit for the view corner. Apply takes the data from the new address, Reset returns the default source. The Add base map…, Edit… and Remove buttons work with the QGIS XYZ Tiles connections, a removed connection disappears from the QGIS browser too. The Terrain - where the heights come from group of the same window explains that the heights are built from four layers - the world height tiles, the 30 m land refinement, the GEBCO sea depths and an own raster of the project. The 30 m land refinement list puts a 30 m terrain model over the height tiles: - No - height tiles only - the Mapzen Terrain Tiles relief, as before. It loads the fastest. North of 60° on land its data is about 250 m. - Copernicus DEM 30 m - the Copernicus GLO-30 surface model, files per degree on the open AWS storage. Forest and buildings are part of the height. - GEDTM30 30 m - the model of the bare ground without forest and buildings, OpenGeoHub, CC BY 4.0. It is one large file, its pieces take longer to read. - ALOS AW3D30 30 m - the JAXA surface model, like Copernicus, forest and buildings are part of the height. - NASADEM 30 m - the improved SRTM without voids, NASA, only between 60° S and 60° N. - USGS 3DEP 10 m - the model of the bare ground without forest and buildings, the USA only. The ALOS, NASADEM and 3DEP files are copies on Microsoft Planetary Computer. The plugin takes a temporary access key to them without an account. Outside the coverage of a model the height tiles remain. The height tiles still give the sea floor and the view from afar. From level 9 the model gives the land heights, deeper than level 12 the model pieces are not read again but resampled from the ones already read. The model credit stands in the view corner. The model is read from the network for every new area, without the network the height tiles remain. At Mount Narodnaya the height tiles give 1816 m, Copernicus and GEDTM30 give 1888 m, ALOS AW3D30 gives 1892 m, the summit is 1895 m. At Pikes Peak in the USA 3DEP gives 4302 m with the summit at 4302 m. The Sea depths list chooses the floor of seas and oceans: - Height tiles - sea floor up to level 10 - the floor from the same Mapzen tiles. Closer than level 10 they have empty spots at zero in the open sea, for example at the Japan Trench. - GEBCO 2026 - a grid of about 450 m - the GEBCO 2026 Grid of world depths, public domain with a credit of the source. From level 5 it replaces the floor of the tiles where both the tile and the grid are below zero, the land and the shore stay from the tiles. The grid is read from the network by areas. This is the default. The label language is chosen from a list. As in QGIS takes the QGIS interface language, Local names keep the names in the language of the country. Fifteen languages follow. When there is no name in the chosen language, Latin-script languages get the Latin name, the others the local one. Labels of a new place load when the camera stops. During a flyover and a flight their loading takes no time from the frames, at a stop they appear in a fraction of a second. Without automatic update a change of base map, terrain exaggeration or project layers shows after the Refresh button on the icon bar. The status line reminds about it. The label language changes at once.

The QGIS project section stands between Places and Layers. It lists the
layers of the current project in the order of the
QGIS map, each with its type - raster, points, lines, polygons, point
cloud or table. The check box of a layer shows it on the globe and does not
change its visibility on the map. In a new project the boxes are clear.
The checks are stored in the project.

Layers lie on the globe as a picture drawn by QGIS, with the styles of
the map. The picture lies on the terrain, it cannot be raised or
extruded.

Labels of vector layers come separately, like city names. They stay
level at any turn and tilt, do not overlap and hide behind mountains
and the horizon. The text, colour and size come from the layer labels
in QGIS, rule-based labels too. A point label stands to the right of
the point, a line label at its middle, a polygon label inside it.
Features around the view point are labelled, at most 500 per layer.
The scale visibility of QGIS labels is not used on the globe.

A double click on a layer flies to its extent, looking straight down.
The right-click menu:

- Fly to - a flight to the extent of the layer.
- Transparency slider - the transparency of the QGIS layer itself, it
  changes on the map too.
- Track… - for point layers, see [Tracks](#tracks).
- Globe terrain - for rasters, see [Own terrain](#own-terrain).
- Extrusion… - for vector layers, see
  [Extrusion by field](#extrusion-by-field).
- To My Places… - for vector layers. The layer features go into My
  Places as a folder named after the layer, the selected ones,
  otherwise all. The folder can then be saved to KML, see
  [KML and KMZ](#kml-and-kmz).
- Point colour, Point size, Point classes - for point clouds, see
  [Point clouds](#point-clouds).
- Layer Properties… - the standard QGIS layer properties window.

A point cloud is a lidar or drone survey in a LAS, LAZ or COPC file. It
is added to the project as an ordinary QGIS point cloud layer and
checked in the QGIS project section. On the globe the cloud stands as
points in space at their own elevations, with depth testing, like 3D
models.

The points are read by the PDAL program shipped with QGIS, in separate
processes, and the window does not wait for them. A COPC file is read
at once. A LAS or LAZ file is converted to COPC once, the copy goes to
the PlanetX/pointclouds folder of the QGIS profile, the source file does
not change. A drone tile of 5.7 million points is converted in about
15 s, later views take the copy.

The detail of the cloud depends on the distance. The cloud is divided
into cells, near cells are smaller and hold more points, far cells the
other way round. A frame holds at most 3 million points. While cells
load, the loading icon to the right of the icon bar is shown.

The elevations of the cloud are converted to metres by the coordinate
system of the file, for example from feet. With terrain the heights are
stretched by the terrain scale, like 3D models, without terrain the
cloud stands with its bottom on the surface. The points are moved
slightly towards the eye, about 0.5 % of the distance. The globe
terrain is smoothed over tens of metres, and without this the ground
points of the survey would go under it.

The menu of a cloud layer:

- Point colour - the survey colour (RGB from the file, without it - by
  class), by ASPRS class, by height from blue to red or by intensity in
  shades of grey.
- Point size - from 1 to 6 pixels.
- Point classes - all classes, ground only or chosen classes among those
  met in the cloud.

The legend in the corner of the view shows the classes of the cloud or
the heights in metres. A click in the Identify features mode gives the
cloud point under the cursor - class, elevation, latitude and longitude,
intensity, return number and colour. The cloud settings are stored in
the project.
Lidar point clouds over the network

The Lidar point clouds here item of the menu on the globe finds tiles
of open lidar surveys at the point and puts them as point cloud layers
into the PlanetX - lidar point clouds group of the project, the layers
are checked on the globe at once. There are two sources:

- IGN LiDAR HD - all of France in 1 km tiles, at least 10 points per
  square metre, ASPRS classes, Licence Ouverte 2.0. The two nearest
  tiles of the point are taken.
- USGS 3DEP - US surveys in tiles of about 1 km, public domain. Up to
  four tiles of the point are taken, one place sometimes has several
  surveys of different years.

The COPC files are not downloaded whole, PDAL and QGIS read them in
parts over the network. The 3DEP files lie in the Microsoft Planetary
Computer storage, the module asks the service for the access key
itself, without an account. The key lives an hour, after that the
layer in the QGIS project stops reading, the globe takes a new key.
The IGN server limits the request rate, so IGN clouds come slower,
cells after a server refusal are asked again in 10 s. Near Grenoble
two IGN tiles give about a million points in 2-3 minutes. Clouds
over the network open in QGIS 4, in QGIS 3.36 opening such a layer
stops QGIS, and the menu item says so.

Features of a project vector layer rise above the terrain to a height
from a numeric field. A polygon becomes a prism, a point an octagonal
column, a line a wall. The Extrusion… item of the layer menu opens a
window with the height field and a factor. The height in metres is
the field value times the factor. For a field of storeys the factor
is about 3. A feature with an empty, zero or negative value is not
extruded. The No extrusion row removes the extrusion.

The colour of a feature is its symbol in the QGIS layer style, as on
the map. The bottom of a prism and a column lies at the lowest terrain
point under the feature, the roof is flat. A line wall follows the
terrain. The column radius is 1/150 of the layer span, from 2 m to
2 km. The layer is extruded while it is checked on the globe. The
settings are kept in the project. Up to 20 000 features of a layer are
read.

A height raster of the QGIS project becomes the globe terrain within
its extent. An example is a quarry with a mine survey. The Globe
terrain item of the raster menu in the QGIS project section turns the
inset on and off. The raster can be in any coordinate system, it needs
a file that GDAL reads. The checkbox that shows the layer on the globe
is not needed for the inset.

Where the raster has data, its heights replace the common terrain.
Along a band at the edge of the data the heights change smoothly to the
common terrain, the band is 5 % of the smaller side of the extent.
Within the extent the terrain is more detailed than the common one,
down to the raster pixel, but not finer than the pixel of level 17
(about 0.6 m at latitude 60°). The raster heights are taken as they
are. If the survey has its own height system, the band at the edge
smooths the difference with the common terrain.

The inset is seen by the surface mesh, the height under the cursor, the
ruler, the elevation profile, the viewshed, the insolation, the slope
and the aspect. With several insets the one higher in the project lies
on top. The choice is kept in the project and in the scene.

On the first switch-on the raster is converted into a file of the QGIS
profile. For a survey of 2400 × 2400 pixels this takes about 2 s.

Two surveys of one site, for example a quarry with dumps, give the cut
and fill volumes. The Cut and fill… item of the menu of the new survey
raster in the QGIS project section opens a window:

- Earlier survey - a raster of the same site at an earlier date.
- Site - polygons outside which the difference is not computed, or the
  whole extent of the new survey.
- Threshold - a difference smaller than the threshold in absolute value
  does not enter the volumes, it is survey noise. The default is 0.1 m.

The earlier survey is resampled to the grid of the new one. The
computation goes in metres, in the coordinate system of the new survey
or in the UTM zone if it is in degrees. The summary window shows the
cut and fill volumes, their areas, the greatest cut depth and fill
height and the difference of the volumes. The difference raster goes
into the project in the PlanetX - cut and fill group and is shown on
the globe, the cut in red, the fill in blue.

A raster of depths or bed elevations of a lake, sea or reservoir goes
into the globe terrain like own terrain, and semi-transparent water at
the water body level is drawn above it. The Water body bathymetry… item
of the raster menu in the QGIS project section opens a window with
three fields:

- Values are depths - the depth below the water surface, with a plus or
  minus sign. The bed elevation is the water level minus the absolute
  depth.
- Values are bed elevations - the bed height above sea level.
- Water level - the height of the water surface. The default is the
  terrain height in the middle of the raster, for a lake it is usually
  the water surface.

The water is drawn over all raster points where the bed is below the
level, the bed is seen through it. Without terrain no water is drawn -
the bed and the water would lie in one plane. Remove bathymetry turns
off both the inset and the water. The choice is kept in the project.
The elevation profile across the water body shows the water above the
bed and a dashed line of the water body level with a label.

The Lake Brienz, own bathymetry demo of the Demo icon is the bed of Lake
Brienz in Switzerland from swisstopo swissBATHY3D data with a 10 m step,
water at 564 m. The deepest point is 308 m, 256 m below the water. The
elevation profile across the lake shows the basin.

Echo sounder soundings are a point layer of the project with the depth
in a field or in the point Z, for example a CSV with latitude,
longitude and depth opened in QGIS as a delimited text layer. The
Bathymetry from soundings… item of the point layer menu builds a depth
raster from them and makes it own bathymetry. The window sets:

- Depth - the field with the depth or the point Z. The sign of the
  depth does not matter.
- Cell - the raster cell size. The default is the square root of the
  sounding area per point. For tracks 20 m apart with a point every
  metre it is 5 m.
- Limit from sounding - a cell farther than this distance from the
  nearest sounding stays empty. The default is 10 cells. The limit has
  to be larger than the distance between tracks.
- Water level - the water height on the day of the soundings.
- File - the GeoTIFF of the depth raster, by default in the QGIS
  profile.

The raster is built by triangulation in metres of the UTM zone of the
middle of the soundings and goes into the project in the PlanetX -
bathymetry group.

The section holds the My Places folder, described in the chapter
[My Places](#my-places).

The synchronization icon on the icon bar links the globe with the QGIS
map window. The direction is chosen in the view properties:

- Both ways - the default.
- Map leads the globe - the globe moves to the map extent and keeps its
  tilt and heading.
- Globe leads the map - the map centers on the look-at point of the
  globe once the globe stops.

Any map coordinate system works. The map width on the ground equals the
width of the globe view.
Features selected on the QGIS map are highlighted on the globe.

The Identify features icon turns identify on, the cursor becomes a
cross. A click on the globe puts a pin with the coordinates and opens
the Features window.

- The top of the window shows the coordinates and elevation of the
  point.
- Below are the project layers checked on the globe, their features
  under the point and the feature fields. A raster shows its values at
  the point.
- The Select on map button selects the found features in the QGIS
  layers. The selection shows on the map, in the attribute table and on
  the globe.
- The My Places group lists the visible placemarks, paths and
  polygons under the point. Each shows its type, coordinates or length,
  measurement and description.
- The Earthquakes group lists the foci near the click point on the
  screen. Each shows its magnitude, depth, UTC time, place and the USGS
  event page.
- The Site group shows the elevation or sea depth, the Moho depth, the
  crust and sediment thickness, the crust type after CRUST1.0 and the
  Slab2 slab under
  the point. The crust model and the slab zone file load on the first
  click, the window updates when they arrive.
